title: God gave the increase (1 Corinthians 3:5–9)

segments.voice: Yesterday, moria: the foolishness of the cross, and a mocking drawing on a Roman wall. Your line was foolish and wise.

Remember Apollos? Eighteen days ago, Priscilla and Aquila took him aside in Ephesus and taught him the way of God more perfectly. Then he crossed to Achaia, Corinth's province, and Acts says he was a great help to the believers there. By the time Paul writes this letter, the church in Corinth has split into fan clubs. I'm with Paul. I'm with Apollos. I'm with Cephas, that is, Peter. And, I'm with Christ. Parishes, teams and families still split this way over favorite people.
screen: `APOLLOS COMES TO CORINTH.` → `I'M WITH PAUL. I'M WITH APOLLOS.` → `A CHURCH OF FAN CLUBS.`

segments.voice: Paul could have used this moment to win; he was the founder. Instead he deflates the whole contest, himself included. Who is Paul, and who is Apollos? Servants, through whom you believed, each doing what the Lord gave him. Then a farmer's picture, in the Douay-Rheims, which spells the name Apollo: "I have planted, Apollo watered, but God gave the increase." Paul put the seed in the ground in Corinth. Apollos came later with the watering can. Both mattered. But neither can make a seed grow; you can only set things up and wait. So: "Therefore, neither he that planteth is any thing, nor he that watereth; but God that giveth the increase." Humbling for the famous preacher, freeing for everyone else. He who plants and he who waters are one, and each will receive his own reward according to his own labor. Then: "For we are God's coadjutors: you are God's husbandry; you are God's building." Coadjutors means co-workers. Husbandry here means a farm, a field under cultivation. The Corinthians aren't anyone's fan club. They're God's field. Notice how gently Paul treats Apollos: not a rival, a co-worker. And notice the honest limit of every worker's job. You can't make your kids believe, your friend heal, your project take off, or your parish grow. You plant, you water, and the increase belongs to God. Catholics reach for this line when their part seems small.
screen: `WHO IS PAUL? WHO IS APOLLOS?` · `ONE PLANTS, ONE WATERS.` · `ONLY GOD MAKES IT GROW.` · `GOD'S CO-WORKERS.` · then, large: `GOD GAVE THE INCREASE.`

segments.voice: Think of something you care about but can't control: a child's faith, a friend's recovery, a project at work, a parish, a garden. Name your one small part in it, planting, watering, or simply not trampling it, and picture setting down the rest, the growing, which was never yours to do. If you pray, hand God the increase, and keep only your watering can.
Coadjutors. Paul's word for himself and Apollos: co-workers who planted and watered, while God alone gave the increase. Today's word.
Your line: god gives the increase. Your part is the planting and the watering. Day five hundred seventy.

what it means: Paul ends a church's fan-club quarrel by saying every worker is a servant, and only God makes anything grow.

what a scholar hears: Paul uses tenses carefully: planted and watered are single past acts, but God was giving the increase all along. and synergoi, co-workers, is the word the Douay-Rheims renders coadjutors.

chat.meaning: In Corinth, Paul deflated the fan clubs: he and Apollos were co-workers, and only God gives the increase.
